core.title: Use a colon for hierarchical descent in artifact names
core.given: A planner is composing, renaming or reviewing an artifact identifier whose segments span different conceptual levels of the resource tree
core.when: choosing or checking the separator where the identifier descends from a more general level to a more specific one
core.then: Use a colon for that hierarchical descent: join the general level and the more specific level beneath it with a colon (general->specific, navigating deeper through organizational subsystems).
prefer: Order segments from general to specific, joined by colons, e.g. a path theme->subsystem->category->item.
Use colons for organizational subsystems and collections as you navigate deeper, e.g. a path domain->collection->type->entity.
avoid: Using a colon between parts that sit on the same conceptual level, which falsely signals descent.
Using another separator (dot, dash, underscore) to step down a level, which hides the hierarchy.
core.why: Hierarchical descent means moving from general to specific down the resource tree, and that movement is marked by a colon.
evidence: Where the planned identifier steps from a parent level to a more specific child level (different conceptual levels), that step is joined by a colon.
Reading the colon-joined levels left to right yields a general->specific path such as theme->subsystem->category->item or domain->collection->type->entity.
verification: No mechanical detector: whether adjacent name segments are different conceptual levels (general->specific) is a semantic judgement with no mechanical observer; the check is reviewer/LLM-judged, and the descent finding alone is sufficient to activate.

What the check looks for: every step between different conceptual levels is joined by a colon, where the colon signals different conceptual levels, navigating deeper, general->specific, organizational subsystems.
Not covered by this check: separators between name segments on the same conceptual level (governed by the related separator-semantics rule), and free-form prose that is not an artifact identifier.

values: an artifact identifier steps from a more general conceptual level to a more specific one (hierarchical descent) and a separator must be chosen or checked at that step

fires: Planner names an artifact whose identifier descends from a theme/domain into a subsystem/collection, then a category/type, then an item/entity.
Planner renames an artifact identifier and must choose the separator between a parent level and the child level beneath it.
Planner or reviewer checks an existing or planned identifier where a deeper, more specific level is joined to its parent.
doesNotFire: Joining words that are on the same conceptual level (e.g. a multi-word name of a single segment) — separator semantics for that case are governed by the related separator-semantics rule.
Work that does not author, rename or review an artifact identifier.
Free-form prose in plan artifacts that is not an artifact identifier.

neutralityNotes: This convention is inherently stack-neutral: it governs the syntax of artifact identifiers (colon as the marker of hierarchical descent) and names no runtime, framework, language, package manager, file suffix or path, so the core is essentially bun.json's obligation verbatim and needs no profile keys (profileRequirements and proposedKeys are empty). Deviations from verbatim: (1) the concrete reference identifiers commons:ux:foundations:color and scenario:catalog:primitives:actor are not repeated in the core (they stay in bun.json, the delivered reference example, and are listed bunOnly); only the conceptual level chains remain; (2) the term id 'hierarchical_descent' and the legacy parity remark in verifier_detail are realization details (bunOnly); (3) the activation fact notes ('illustrative cue only, not a gate', 'sufficient on its own to activate') have no field in the core facts schema — the sufficiency/no-observer point is carried by core.verification, and the cue-not-gate point is recorded in the classification notes; bun.json remains authoritative for those nuances; (4) 'plan docs' in doesNotFire was rendered as 'plan artifacts' to use the role vocabulary, with identical meaning.
